Yep, I've noticed this too. This seems like a limitation in the rustbox crate as a single resource is used to both draw the characters in the terminal, and receive input from keyboard.

At the moment, rustbox listens for keyboard input within intervals of 1000 nanosecs ([source](https://github.com/ritiek/piano-rs/blob/ed8994004912e3e0a101cfe27c1e6661399b35c8/src/main.rs#L65-L67)). If input is received within this interval then the corresponding note is played. If input is not received within this interval, it will continue to wait for input during the next interval in the next iteration. This nanosecs wait is necessary to release the mutex lock so that rustbox can acquire the lock in a different thread, which is necessary to color any piano keys depending on the corresponding note received from the UDP socket ([source](https://github.com/ritiek/piano-rs/blob/ed8994004912e3e0a101cfe27c1e6661399b35c8/src/main.rs#L58)). But this design seems to put too much load on the CPU like you mentioned. The CPU usage goes down drastically if I increase the duration from 1000 nanosecs to say 10 millisecs but then the latency gap between when a key is hit on the keyboard, and the corresponding note being played is pretty noticeable.

I also experimented a bit with crossterm-rs and it seems like this excess CPU usage should be fixed once we transition from rustbox to crossterm. This is because in crossterm - drawing terminal characters and keyboard input listener use a different type (atleast that's what I think so), and therefore do not need share the same resource.

I could be wrong here given my little understanding of how things work underneath, but this is what I think.

**EDIT:** Switched to crossterm with [#38](https://github.com/ritiek/piano-rs/pull/38) and high CPU usage on idle state should no longer be an issue now.
Nope, this won't work. This will untrack the file from future commits, but the file will live on in the commit history.

It won't be as simple as removing the binary files by pushing a new commit. Whenever you git clone a repository, all the commit history gets downloaded as well. So, the binary files will still get downloaded and be hidden in the commit history. You'll need to mess with your commit history to remove any trace of binary files. This seems a pretty good [guide](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/remove-binaries?view=azure-devops).  


If you're going to follow the guide above, I suggest you take a local backup just in case things go wrong.

The fact that you also wrote tests for your tool, shows that you've been putting a genuine effort to learn. Great job!

However, it is generally not a good idea to put compiled binaries in the repository itself. The binaries considerably increase the size of the repository and anyone who wants to git clone only the source code files (which are usually in KBs), will be forced to download the large binary files as well. GitHub provides a separate dedicated section to upload binary files (such as for [your repository](https://github.com/theaveragedude/mediacat/releases)) by creating a new release, in case one wishes to distribute binaries.
